subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: deciding a personal rule for what counts as own work [Thinking]
passage: Irfan pulled up the school's technology policy on the laptop before dinner and read the paragraph on AI twice. Explaining ideas: allowed. Graded work: must be your own. That part was clear. Now for his own rule. He wrote in his notebook: AI may explain a topic I don't get. AI may check an answer after I've written it. AI may not write anything I hand in. He thought about the history essay due Friday. If the tool wrote a paragraph, whose thinking would that be? Not his. If it explained the causes of the revolt and he wrote them in his own words, that was his. Wasim texted: just let it write the intro, nobody checks. Irfan replied: I know. I'd know. He closed the chat and started the outline.

qa.q: What did Irfan read twice?
qa.a: Irfan read the paragraph on AI in the school's technology policy twice.

qa.q: How does Irfan seem to feel about Wasim's suggestion?
qa.a: Irfan seems resolute and self-respecting, since he calmly answers I'd know and starts the outline.

qa.q: What could Irfan do if he gets stuck on the essay?
qa.a: Irfan could ask the tool to explain the causes in simpler words, or ask the teacher what is allowed, then write it himself.

qa.q: How might Wasim see Irfan's rule?
qa.a: Wasim may find it strict, since nobody checks, but may also feel a nudge to think about his own use.

grounding: A student decides AI may explain ideas and check his work but written answers must be his own, and reads the school policy to confirm the line.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: using AI as a tutor by asking for explanations [Action]
passage:
Monday. Deepika stared at x² + 5x + 6 = 0 for twenty minutes. The textbook's steps might as well have been in another language. She was close to tears when her brother Eshaan said, “Ask the AI to explain it like you're twelve.” She did, and it broke the steps into small pieces: find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5.
Wednesday. She asked for five practice questions and solved them all on paper before looking at the answers. Three right, two wrong. She asked why the wrong ones were wrong.
Saturday. Class test. Deepika solved four equations with no phone in sight and got three right. She told Eshaan, “It didn't do it for me. It sat next to me while I did it.”

qa.q: How many practice questions did Deepika ask for?
qa.a: Deepika asked for five practice questions.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel on Monday?
qa.a: Deepika felt frustrated and close to tears after twenty minutes with no progress.

qa.q: What could Deepika do if the tool's explanation is still unclear?
qa.a: Deepika could ask her teacher or ask the tool to explain in a different way, since another route may click when the first does not.

qa.q: How might Eshaan see her progress?
qa.a: Eshaan is probably pleased, since his suggestion helped, and her sentence about the tool sitting next to her shows she did the work.

grounding: A teen stuck on quadratic equations asks an AI to explain the steps simply and give practice questions, then solves them herself and checks afterwards.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: attempting first, then asking for feedback [Action]
passage: Teacher's note, Shalini. Ankit brought his essay draft on Tuesday with a page of comments in the margin. He had written the whole first draft himself, then asked an AI tool two questions: which parts were unclear, and how the structure could be tighter. He did not paste in any of its sentences. The tool said his second paragraph jumped between two ideas, so he split it and rewrote both halves in his own words. He showed me both versions. The second draft was clearer, and, more importantly, he could explain why. I asked how he decided what to keep from the feedback, and he said he kept whatever made sense to him. I have told him that this order, own thinking first and feedback second, is a good habit for other subjects too.

qa.q: Which two questions did Ankit ask the tool?
qa.a: Ankit asked which parts were unclear and how the structure could be tighter.

qa.q: What might Ankit feel when he explains why the second draft is clearer?
qa.a: Ankit probably feels proud and confident, since he understands the changes as his own.

qa.q: What could Ankit do if the tool's feedback is confusing?
qa.a: Ankit could check with Shalini or a classmate, since a person who knows the assignment can say which comments to keep.

qa.q: How might Shalini see this way of working?
qa.a: Shalini sees own thinking first and feedback second as a good habit, and wants to encourage it in other subjects.

grounding: A student writes his own essay draft, then asks an AI what is unclear and how to improve the structure, and rewrites the text himself.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: verifying AI answers against sources [Action]
passage:
In the school library, Trisha typed her history question into an AI tool: when did the Battle of Plassey take place? It answered 1758 in confident, neat sentences. She began copying it into her notes, then paused. The textbook was on the desk. She flipped to chapter six: 1757. She checked the index, then the timeline on page 84. Both said 1757. Ramesh Sir, the librarian, passed with a trolley and glanced over. “Something wrong?”
“The AI gave me a different date from the book.”
“Which do you trust for an exam?”
“The book. And I should confirm with a second source. It can make mistakes.”
She crossed out 1758, wrote 1757 with a star, and added at the top of the page: AI is a starting point, not the final answer.

qa.q: What date did the AI give?
qa.a: The AI answered 1758.

qa.q: How does Trisha feel about the AI after finding the error?
qa.a: Trisha feels wary and more careful, since she now treats the tool as fallible and wants a second source.

qa.q: What could Trisha do to check other facts?
qa.a: Trisha could compare the textbook, its index and timeline, or ask a teacher or the librarian, since reliable sources can confirm a claim.

qa.q: How might Ramesh Sir see what Trisha did?
qa.a: Ramesh Sir is probably pleased that a student checked, and his question about which she trusts invites her to use her own reasoning.

grounding: A student checks a historical date the AI gave against the textbook, finds an error and learns to treat the tool as fallible.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: copying AI output as homework [Pitfall]
passage: On Sunday night, with three questions left and her eyes drooping, Damini pasted the science question into an AI tool, copied its neat paragraph about the water cycle into her notebook and went to bed. On Monday she handed in the homework and felt clever. On Wednesday Yusuf Sir asked her to explain, in her own words, why water vapour condenses higher up. Damini's mouth opened; nothing came. She could remember the shape of the paragraph, not its meaning. The class waited in silence. On Friday the test had a similar question with different numbers, and she stared at the page. She wrote two half-sentences and put her pen down. She got 4 out of 10. It wasn't that she couldn't learn it; the learning simply never happened.

qa.q: What did Damini do on Sunday night?
qa.a: Damini pasted the science question into an AI tool and copied its neat paragraph into her notebook.

qa.q: How did Damini feel on Wednesday when asked to explain?
qa.a: Damini felt embarrassed and stuck, since her mouth opened and nothing came.

qa.q: What could Damini try next time?
qa.a: Damini could ask the tool to explain the idea, then write her own answer, or ask Yusuf Sir for help, since explaining in her own words makes the learning happen.

qa.q: How might Yusuf Sir see that moment in class?
qa.a: Yusuf Sir probably becomes concerned and realises she has not really learned it, since she cannot explain what her homework says.

grounding: A teen pastes an AI-written answer as homework, then cannot explain it in class or solve a similar problem on the test, since the learning never happened.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: reasoning that everyone does it [Pitfall]
passage:
On the bench outside the tea shop in the small town, after Class 10 tuition, Anand held up his phone. “Everyone's using AI for the essays. Half of 10-B. So it's fine.”
Ishita frowned. “Sir said the assignment has to be your own.”
“Sir doesn't know how many do it. If everybody does, that's basically the rule.” He liked that sentence and repeated it in his head all the way home. He pasted the prompt, submitted the answer and felt good. Then Ishita's essay, stumbling and honest, got 7 marks and his got 9 for no effort of his own, and he felt a small, unpleasant pinch. He shrugged it off. Later, when the teacher asked him to write two lines on the topic in class, he found he couldn't.

qa.q: What did Anand say about the rest of the class?
qa.a: Anand said everyone is using AI for the essays, half of 10-B.

qa.q: What might Anand's small pinch mean?
qa.a: Anand may feel uneasy and a little guilty, sensing it is not fair that his effortless answer beat Ishita's honest one.

qa.q: What could Anand do differently?
qa.a: Anand could follow the school's rule, use AI only to explain ideas and write the essay himself, since a crowd's habit does not change fairness or his own learning.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel about the marks?
qa.a: Ishita may feel frustrated or unfairly treated, since Ishita's honest work earned fewer marks than an answer with no effort.

grounding: A student argues that classmates already use AI for assignments, so it must be fine, and ignores school rules, fairness and his own skill development.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: being open with the teacher about use [Action]
passage:
Dear Pema Ma'am,
Before I submit my essay on climate and farming, I wanted to tell you how I used an AI tool. I asked it for five angles I could take, and I picked the one on water use. I also asked it to point out grammar mistakes, and I fixed them myself. All the sentences and arguments are mine, and I have attached my rough notes so you can see how the essay grew. I wasn't sure if this is within the rules for the assignment, so I would like to ask you directly. If any of it is not allowed, I'm happy to change it before you mark it. P.S. I would rather ask now than have you wonder later.
Yours sincerely,
Parveen

qa.q: What did Parveen ask the AI tool to do?
qa.a: Parveen asked it for five angles and to point out grammar mistakes.

qa.q: Why did Parveen write to Pema Ma'am before submitting?
qa.a: Parveen was unsure whether it is within the rules, and feels honest but a little nervous, wanting to keep the teacher's trust.

qa.q: What could Parveen do if Pema Ma'am says part of it is not allowed?
qa.a: Parveen could redo that part without the tool and ask what help is acceptable, as the email offers.

qa.q: How might Pema Ma'am see the email?
qa.a: Pema Ma'am is likely to appreciate the openness, since it is easier to guide a student who says how the tool was used.

grounding: A teen tells the teacher the AI was used to brainstorm ideas and check grammar, shows the notes and asks whether that fits the rules.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: testing understanding without the tool [Revision]
passage: Tutor's note, Hemant. Mridul came in on Thursday and said something I liked: “I notice I open the AI before I try the problem.” He had decided to test himself. He closed it, took a fresh problem like last week's, and tried it cold for fifteen minutes. He got stuck at the second step and saw that he could not remember how to set up the equation, something he had let the tool do all month. He wrote down the gap and set a rule for himself: a fair attempt first, twenty minutes; only then ask for a hint, never the answer. We went over the gap together. Next week he will show me his attempts before asking for help. I told him that noticing this on his own is the harder part.

qa.q: How long did Mridul try the problem without the tool?
qa.a: Mridul tried it cold for fifteen minutes.

qa.q: How does Mridul probably feel on seeing the gap?
qa.a: Mridul probably feels uneasy but honest, and determined to fix it, since he wrote down the gap and set a rule.

qa.q: What could Mridul do to make the rule stick?
qa.a: Mridul could show his attempts to Hemant and note where a hint was needed, since a record keeps the habit honest.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Mridul's self-test?
qa.a: Hemant is encouraged, since noticing the dependence alone is the harder part.

grounding: After noticing he depends on AI, a student closes it, tries a similar problem cold, sees gaps and asks for hints only after a fair attempt.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: correcting course after crossing the line [Revision]
passage: I'm Aditi, and I'll be honest: I submitted a history assignment that was about ninety percent AI. I told myself I'd rewrite it later. I didn't. Three days later the class was discussing my topic and I couldn't say a word, and I felt sick, not because I might get caught, but because it wasn't mine. That evening I decided to tell Yusuf Sir before anyone asked. I walked to the staffroom with cold hands and said it straight. He was quiet, then said, “Thank you for telling me, beti.” I would lose the marks for that submission and had to redo it. I said, “I know.” I rewrote it that week in my own words, slowly and badly at first. And I made a rule: AI can explain, never write. The mark was lower. But I can talk about that topic now.

qa.q: What did Aditi decide to do that evening?
qa.a: Aditi decided to tell Yusuf Sir before anyone asked.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she could not say a word in class?
qa.a: Aditi felt sick with guilt, since the work was not hers.

qa.q: Which choice worked in Aditi's story, and why?
qa.a: Telling the teacher and redoing the work in her own words worked, because it fixed the problem and the learning finally happened.

qa.q: How might Yusuf Sir see Aditi's confession?
qa.a: Yusuf Sir probably appreciates her honesty, since he thanks her, even as he applies the consequence.

grounding: A teen who submitted mostly AI-written work realises it was wrong, tells the teacher, redoes it in her own words and sets a rule, accepting a consequence.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: protecting privacy when using AI [Thinking]
passage: Sohan was about to paste his whole profile into an AI tool to get tips for his science-fair speech: full name, address, school, marks from the last exam. His cursor hovered. Gurpreet leaned in. “Wait, you're putting your address in there?” Sohan stopped. He didn't know where the information went, who could read it, or how long it stayed. He deleted the first lines. I'll say: a Class 10 student, speech on solar cookers. No name, no address, no marks, no friends' names. He also removed a line about Gurpreet's project. He typed the general version and still got useful tips. On a sticky note on his monitor he wrote: Ask about ideas, not about me.

qa.q: What did Sohan write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Sohan wrote: Ask about ideas, not about me.

qa.q: What made Sohan stop and delete the details?
qa.a: Sohan felt uneasy because he did not know where the information went, who could read it or how long it stayed.

qa.q: What else could Sohan do to stay safe with such tools?
qa.a: Sohan could ask a parent or teacher about privacy settings before using a tool for anything personal.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's privacy have been affected if the project line stayed in?
qa.a: Gurpreet's project details would have been shared without permission, so removing the line protects Gurpreet.

grounding: A student decides not to enter his full name, address, marks or friends' details into an AI tool, since he does not know how the information is stored or used.
